The bug that started it The issue behind this PR was deceptively small: torch.ops.aten.index.Tensor(t, []) could crash instead of failing cleanly when the index list was empty. In other words, PyTorch was being asked to perform tensor indexing with no actual indices, and one of the internal code paths did not defend itself against that case.
That sounds like a corner case, but it is exactly the kind of corner case that matters in a system like PyTorch. Indexing is one of the most heavily used operations in the entire stack, and even a tiny inconsistency can surface in surprising places, especially once you start mixing Python frontend code, ATen internals, and backend-specific behavior.
From Python syntax to ATen internals When you write something like x[0] in Python, the operation does not stay in Python for long. It is lowered into ATen, PyTorch’s internal tensor library, where the framework decides how to interpret the indexing request and which backend should handle it.
That path has to answer a lot of questions:
Is the index list valid? Are we doing basic or advanced indexing? Do the indices describe a contiguous subspace? Should the implementation materialize any optional indices first? The bug in this PR lived in that validation layer. The problem was not really about a specific device or dtype. It was about what happens when the list of indices is empty and the internal helpers assume there is at least one meaningful tensor to inspect.
The fix The PR made two functional changes in the C++ code and one regression test in Python.
First, IndexingUtils.h was updated so that the helper that checks whether the indexed tensors form a contiguous subspace handles an empty set safely. That is the kind of guard that looks boring in isolation, but it is exactly what keeps an internal helper from wandering into undefined behavior when the input is degenerate.
Second, TensorAdvancedIndexing.cpp now checks the meta path for an empty index list and raises a clear IndexError with the message at least one index must be provided. That is the right failure mode here: fail early, fail explicitly, and fail in a place that tells the caller what is wrong.
Third, the Python test suite gained a regression test that exercises the exact empty-index call:
with self.assertRaisesRegex(IndexError, "at least one index must be provided"): torch.ops.aten.index.Tensor(t, []) That test is doing more than checking an error message. It locks in the contract so the bug does not quietly return later after some unrelated refactor.
Why this matters The best bug fixes in systems code are usually the ones that make an invalid state impossible to ignore. This PR does not add a new feature. It makes an existing path trustworthy.
That matters because PyTorch is built on layers of assumptions. Python frontend code assumes ATen will validate correctly. ATen assumes its helpers can reason about the shape and structure of the index inputs. Backends assume the higher layers have already rejected nonsense before dispatch reaches them. A missing guard at any one layer can turn a harmless user mistake into a crash.
This fix restores the expected contract:
empty indices are not accepted here, the error is explicit, and the test suite now protects that behavior. What I learned This PR was a good reminder that most of the work in framework code is not glamorous dispatch wizardry. It is defensive engineering.
The interesting part is rarely the final TORCH_CHECK_INDEX itself. It is understanding where the check belongs so that the failure is caught at the correct abstraction layer. In this case, the right answer was not to let a helper stumble through an empty input and hope later code would catch it. The right answer was to make the empty-input contract obvious as soon as the indexing path is entered.
That is the kind of fix that feels small in a diff, but it has a real effect on the reliability of the whole stack.
Closing thought tensor[0] looks simple from Python, but it only works because a lot of C++ code makes careful decisions on your behalf. This PR was a tiny example of that machinery doing exactly what it should: refusing an invalid indexing request cleanly instead of crashing somewhere deeper in the stack.
That is the kind of internal behavior that users usually never notice, which is exactly the point.

with self.assertRaisesRegex(IndexError, "at least one index must be provided"): torch.ops.aten.index.Tensor(t, []) That test is doing more than checking an error message. It locks in the contract so the bug does not quietly return later after some unrelated refactor.
summary:
Whenever we write tensor[0] in Python, it feels like magic. But under the hood, PyTorch has to route this operation through a massive C++ dispatching engine to figure out if this should run on a CPU or a CUDA GPU…

The Bug: Empty Indices Crashing index.Tensor

The issue behind this PR was deceptively small: torch.ops.aten.index.Tensor(t, []) could crash instead of failing cleanly when the index list was empty. In other words, PyTorch was being asked to perform tensor indexing with no actual indices, and one of the internal code paths did not defend itself against that case.
title: Deconstructing my PyTorch ATen PR: What happens when you index a Tensor?
